callouts.p: For every 'give a use' question, add 'because...' and state the property, e.g. 'X-rays are used to image bones because they are absorbed by bone but transmitted by soft tissue.'

core.h: Radio waves: broadcasting and communication
core.p: Radio waves have the **longest wavelengths** (from about a metre to kilometres). They are produced by oscillating currents in an aerial and can induce an oscillating current in a receiving aerial, which is how a radio or TV signal is carried.
bullets: Used for **TV and radio broadcasting**, two-way radio and wireless communication.
**Long-wave** radio diffracts (bends) around hills and the curve of the Earth, so it can be received a long way from the transmitter.
**Short-wave** radio can reflect off the **ionosphere** (a charged layer of the upper atmosphere), so it can reach distant countries.
Shorter radio wavelengths used for FM radio and TV need a clear **line of sight** between transmitter and receiver.
Radio waves pass through walls and are **not absorbed by the body** in a harmful way, so they are safe for everyday use.

callouts.p: Long wavelength means radio waves diffract around obstacles and are not strongly absorbed by the atmosphere, so the signal travels a long way.

core.h: Microwaves: satellites, phones and cooking
core.p: Microwaves have wavelengths from about a millimetre to about 30 cm. Two very different uses come from two different properties.
bullets: **Satellite communication** (satellite TV, GPS) and **mobile phone** networks use microwaves because they **pass through the atmosphere** (including cloud and rain) without being significantly absorbed or reflected.
Satellite signals travel in straight lines, so a dish must point directly at the satellite.
**Microwave ovens** use microwaves of a wavelength that is strongly **absorbed by water molecules** in food.
The absorbed energy makes the water molecules vibrate more, increasing the **internal energy** (temperature) of the food.
Microwaves penetrate a few centimetres into food, so food is heated inside as well as on the surface.
The metal walls and door mesh of a microwave oven **reflect** microwaves, keeping them inside.

callouts.p: Microwave ovens do not make food radioactive. Microwaves are non-ionising; they only increase the thermal energy of the water in the food.

core.h: Infrared: heating, thermal imaging and remote controls
core.p: All objects emit infrared radiation, and hotter objects emit more of it. Infrared is also absorbed by the surfaces of most materials, which makes them warmer.
bullets: **Cooking**: grills, toasters and ovens transfer energy by infrared, which is absorbed by the **surface** of the food (unlike microwaves which penetrate further).
**Electric heaters** emit infrared to warm a room.
**Thermal imaging cameras** detect the infrared emitted by objects; warmer objects show up brighter. Used by police, search and rescue, and to find heat loss from houses.
**Night-vision** equipment uses infrared emitted by warm bodies.
**Remote controls** send pulses of infrared to the TV; the pattern of pulses is a code for each button.
**Optical fibres** can carry infrared signals for data and telephone communication.

callouts.p: Microwaves penetrate deeper and are absorbed by water; infrared is absorbed mainly at the surface, so grilled food browns on the outside first.

core.h: Visible light: vision, photography and fibre optics
core.p: Visible light is the only region the human eye can detect. Its uses come from that and from its ability to travel along glass fibres.
bullets: **Vision** and **illumination**: lamps and screens emit visible light so that we can see.
**Photography**: the camera lens focuses visible light onto a sensor or film.
**Fibre optic communication**: pulses of light (or infrared) travel along thin glass fibres by **total internal reflection**, carrying data such as broadband internet.
Optical fibres carry a lot of data, with little energy loss, and signals are hard to intercept.
Medical **endoscopes** use bundles of optical fibres to see inside the body without major surgery.

callouts.p: In an optical fibre the light hits the glass boundary at a large angle and is completely reflected back inside, so it zig-zags along the fibre even round bends.

core.h: Ultraviolet: fluorescence, security and sterilising
core.p: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency than visible light, so it carries more energy. Some chemicals absorb ultraviolet and then **emit visible light**; this is called **fluorescence**.
bullets: **Fluorescent lamps** and energy-efficient lamps: UV is produced inside the tube and absorbed by a coating which glows with visible light.
**Security marking**: invisible ink glows under UV light, so marked property or banknotes can be checked.
**Sterilising water** and equipment: UV has enough energy to kill bacteria and other microbes.
**Sun tanning** beds use UV to make the skin produce more melanin (a hazard as well as a use).
Detecting forged banknotes, which lack the correct fluorescent marks.

callouts.p: When a substance absorbs ultraviolet radiation and re-emits the energy as visible light.

core.h: X-rays: medical imaging and security
core.p: X-rays have very short wavelengths and high frequencies. Their key property is that different materials **absorb** them by different amounts.
bullets: **Medical X-ray images**: X-rays are **transmitted** through soft tissue (skin, muscle) but **absorbed** by dense materials such as **bone**.
A detector plate behind the patient turns dark where X-rays reach it, so bones appear as white shadows.
**CT scans** combine many X-ray images from different angles to make a 3D picture.
**Airport security**: X-rays scan luggage; metal objects absorb X-rays and show clearly.
Also used to check for cracks in metal welds and structures.
Because X-rays are **ionising**, staff leave the room or stand behind lead screens and the patient's dose is kept as low as possible.

callouts.p: 'X-rays are absorbed by bone but pass through (are transmitted by) soft tissue.'

core.h: Gamma rays: radiotherapy, sterilising and tracers
core.p: Gamma rays have the highest frequency and energy. They are **very penetrating** and their energy can **kill living cells**, which is useful when the cells are cancer cells or bacteria.
bullets: **Radiotherapy**: beams of gamma rays are aimed at a tumour from several directions so the tumour gets a high dose but the surrounding healthy tissue gets less.
**Sterilising medical equipment**: sealed packs of syringes and instruments are exposed to gamma rays, which kill all microbes; the pack stays sealed so it remains sterile.
**Sterilising food** (irradiation): kills bacteria so food lasts longer; the food does not become radioactive.
**Medical tracers**: a gamma-emitting substance is put into the body; gamma rays pass out of the body and are detected by a camera to show how an organ is working.
Gamma rays are used because they pass through packaging and the body easily.

callouts.p: Food or equipment exposed to gamma rays is irradiated, not contaminated. It does not become radioactive.

core.h: Choosing the right wave: linking to absorption and transmission
core.p: The underlying reason behind every use is how strongly a material absorbs, transmits or reflects that wavelength. Grade 9 answers name the interaction.
bullets: Communication needs waves that are **transmitted** by the atmosphere (radio, microwave) or by glass (visible, infrared).
Heating needs waves that are **absorbed** by the material to be heated (infrared by surfaces, microwaves by water).
Imaging needs waves that are absorbed **differently** by different materials (X-rays: bone v soft tissue).
Sterilising and cancer treatment need waves with enough energy to **damage cells** (UV, gamma).
Detection and tracers need waves that are **transmitted** out of the body (gamma).

callouts.p: Structure: name the wave, state the use, explain the property (absorbed / transmitted / energy), then mention any safety precaution.

core.h: Benefits versus risks
core.p: Using the high-frequency end of the spectrum always involves weighing benefits against hazards. The hazards themselves are covered in P5.2h, but uses questions often ask you to justify a use.
bullets: A single X-ray carries a very small risk, which is outweighed by the benefit of a correct diagnosis.
Radiotherapy can cause side effects because some healthy cells are also damaged; the benefit of destroying the tumour is greater.
Radio waves, microwaves at low intensity, infrared and visible light are **non-ionising**, so everyday communication uses are low risk.
Workers who use X-rays and gamma rays repeatedly must limit their own exposure using shielding, distance and time.

callouts.p: Ultraviolet (high frequency), X-rays and gamma rays are ionising; radio, microwaves, infrared and visible light are not.

analogy.p: Think of the EM spectrum as a bunch of keys of different sizes. Each material is a lock that only certain keys open: water 'opens' for microwaves (absorbs them), bone 'opens' for X-rays, the atmosphere lets radio and microwaves pass. Picking the right wave for a job is like picking the key that fits. The analogy breaks down because a material does not simply open or stay shut: it absorbs a fraction of the wave, and all the 'keys' are really the same kind of wave differing only in wavelength and frequency.

terms.d: The continuous range of electromagnetic waves ordered by wavelength or frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
When a material takes in the energy of a wave, usually increasing its internal energy.
When a wave passes through a material.
When a wave bounces back from a boundary between two materials.
The spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle; greatest for long wavelengths such as radio.
A layer of charged particles in the upper atmosphere that can reflect some radio waves.
Using microwaves to send signals to and from satellites because microwaves pass through the atmosphere.
Forming an image from the infrared radiation emitted by objects; hotter objects emit more infrared.
A thin glass fibre that carries visible light or infrared by total internal reflection.
Complete reflection of light at a boundary when it hits it at an angle greater than the critical angle, from a denser medium.
Absorption of ultraviolet radiation by a substance which then emits visible light.
Killing all bacteria and other microbes on equipment or food, for example using UV or gamma rays.
Treating cancer by directing ionising radiation such as gamma rays at a tumour to kill the cancer cells.
A gamma-emitting substance put into the body so that its path can be followed by a detector outside the body.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, forming ions; includes UV, X-rays and gamma rays.

mistakes.w: Microwaves cook food by making it radioactive.
mistakes.r: Microwaves are absorbed by water molecules, increasing their kinetic energy so the food gets hotter; the food is not radioactive.

mistakes.w: X-rays are reflected by bones.
mistakes.r: X-rays are absorbed by bone and transmitted through soft tissue.

mistakes.w: Satellites use radio waves because they reflect off the ionosphere.
mistakes.r: Satellite communication uses microwaves because they pass through the atmosphere and ionosphere to reach the satellite.

mistakes.w: Thermal imaging cameras send out infrared and detect it bouncing back.
mistakes.r: They detect infrared emitted by the objects themselves; warmer objects emit more.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays are used to sterilise because they are hot.
mistakes.r: Gamma rays have high energy and are ionising, so they kill microbes; they pass through the sealed packaging.

mistakes.w: UV lamps make things glow because UV is visible.
mistakes.r: UV is invisible; fluorescent chemicals absorb UV and emit visible light.

mistakes.w: Giving a use without a reason.
mistakes.r: Mark schemes usually give a second mark for the property, e.g. 'because it passes through the atmosphere'.

mistakes.w: Optical fibres work by refraction along the fibre.
mistakes.r: Light travels along optical fibres by total internal reflection.

exam.q: State one use of microwaves.
model: Any one: satellite communication / mobile phones / cooking food / radar.
exam.tip: One clear use is enough for 1 mark; do not list several with one wrong.

exam.q: Explain why X-rays can be used to produce an image of a broken bone.
model: X-rays are absorbed by bone.
X-rays are transmitted through (pass through) soft tissue, so a shadow of the bone forms on the detector.
exam.tip: Use both words 'absorbed' and 'transmitted'.

exam.q: Explain why microwaves, rather than radio waves, are used to communicate with satellites.
model: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere / ionosphere.
Some radio waves are reflected by the ionosphere so would not reach the satellite.
exam.tip: Compare the two waves directly.

exam.q: Describe how a microwave oven heats food.
model: Microwaves are absorbed by water molecules in the food.
The water molecules vibrate more / gain kinetic energy.
Energy is transferred to the rest of the food by conduction so the temperature rises.
exam.tip: Mention water specifically.

exam.q: Give two uses of infrared radiation.
model: Any two: cooking / grills / toasters; thermal imaging cameras; remote controls; electric heaters; optical fibre communication; night vision.
exam.tip: Avoid vague answers like 'heat'.

exam.q: Explain how gamma rays are used to sterilise surgical instruments.
model: Instruments are sealed in packaging then exposed to gamma rays.
Gamma rays pass through the packaging (very penetrating).
Gamma rays kill bacteria / microbes because they are high energy / ionising.
Instruments stay sterile until the pack is opened.
exam.tip: Any three points; the sealed pack point is often missed.

exam.q: Ultraviolet lamps are used to check banknotes. Explain how this works.
model: Real banknotes have marks printed in fluorescent ink.
The ink absorbs ultraviolet and emits visible light, so the mark glows; forgeries do not glow.
exam.tip: Name fluorescence.

exam.q: State which type of electromagnetic wave is used in optical fibre communication and state how it travels along the fibre.
model: Visible light or infrared.
By total internal reflection.
exam.tip: Either light or infrared is accepted.

exam.q: Describe and explain uses of three different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in medicine. Include the property that makes each suitable.
model: X-rays used to image bones / CT scans.
Because X-rays are absorbed by bone but transmitted by soft tissue.
Gamma rays used in radiotherapy to kill cancer cells / to sterilise equipment.
Because gamma rays are highly penetrating and ionising, so kill cells / microbes.
Ultraviolet used to sterilise / visible light in endoscopes (optical fibres) / infrared thermal imaging for inflammation.
Correct matching property, e.g. endoscope light travels by total internal reflection; precautions such as minimising dose.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs three regions, each with use AND reason, in a logical order.

exam.q: Long-wave radio can be received behind hills but TV signals often cannot. Explain why.
model: Long-wave radio has a long wavelength so diffracts around hills.
TV uses shorter wavelengths which diffract very little, so they need line of sight.
exam.tip: Link wavelength to amount of diffraction.

worked.q: A student says 'Microwaves and infrared both cook food in the same way.' Evaluate this statement.
steps: Both transfer energy to the food, which is absorbed and increases its thermal energy store, so they are similar.
Microwaves are absorbed by water molecules and penetrate a few centimetres into the food, heating it inside.
Infrared is absorbed mainly by the surface of the food; the inside is heated by conduction from the surface.
So the statement is only partly correct.
worked.ans: Partly correct: both heat food by absorption, but microwaves penetrate and are absorbed by water inside, while infrared is absorbed at the surface.

worked.q: A hospital needs (a) to see a fractured wrist, (b) to destroy a tumour, and (c) to look inside a patient's stomach without surgery. Choose a wave for each and justify.
steps: (a) X-rays: absorbed by bone, transmitted through soft tissue, so the fracture shows on the image.
(b) Gamma rays: high energy and penetrating; beams from several directions concentrate the dose on the tumour and kill cancer cells.
(c) Visible light in an endoscope: light travels along optical fibres by total internal reflection, carrying an image out of the body.
worked.ans: (a) X-rays, (b) gamma rays, (c) visible light in optical fibres (endoscope), each justified by its property.

phy_ocra.12.3.summary: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are at the high-frequency end of the electromagnetic spectrum, so they transfer the most energy and are hazardous to living tissue. Ultraviolet damages surface cells and the eyes, causing sunburn, premature skin ageing, skin cancer and eye conditions such as cataracts. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and penetrate deep into the body, where they can damage or kill cells and cause mutations in DNA that may lead to cancer. The size of the hazard depends on the frequency (energy) of the radiation, the dose and how long a person is exposed.

core.h: Why the high-frequency end is hazardous
core.p: The energy carried by an electromagnetic wave increases as its **frequency increases** (and wavelength decreases). Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have high enough frequencies to transfer enough energy to damage the molecules inside living cells.
bullets: Order of increasing frequency and energy: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, **ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma**.
The higher the frequency, the more energy is transferred, and the greater the potential for damage.
These three can cause **ionisation**: they knock electrons out of atoms or molecules.
Lower-frequency waves (radio, microwave, infrared, visible) are **non-ionising**; their main hazard is heating at high intensity.

callouts.p: Higher frequency means more energy transferred, so ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are the most hazardous to living cells.

core.h: Ionising radiation
core.p: An ion is an atom or molecule that has gained or lost electrons. When ionising radiation passes through a cell it can remove electrons from atoms in molecules such as **DNA**, leaving charged ions. These ions are very reactive and can break chemical bonds.
bullets: Ionisation can **damage DNA** in the cell nucleus.
Damaged DNA can cause a **mutation**: the cell's genetic instructions are changed.
A mutated cell may divide uncontrollably, forming a **tumour**: this is **cancer**.
A large dose can **kill cells** outright (radiation burns, radiation sickness).
Ionisation is the reason X-rays and gamma rays can harm cells deep inside the body.

callouts.p: Radiation that has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, producing ions.

core.h: Hazards of ultraviolet
core.p: Ultraviolet is mostly absorbed by the outer layers of skin and the front of the eye, so its damage is to **surface cells**.
bullets: **Sunburn**: UV damages and kills skin cells, causing redness and pain.
**Premature ageing** of the skin (wrinkles, loss of elasticity).
**Skin cancer**: UV can cause mutations in the DNA of skin cells.
**Eye damage**: UV can damage the cornea and lens, leading to eye conditions such as **cataracts** (clouding of the lens) and snow blindness.
Sources: the Sun, sunbeds, welding arcs and UV lamps.
Darker skin contains more melanin, which absorbs UV and gives some protection; tanning is the skin making more melanin in response to damage.

callouts.p: Ultraviolet can damage surface cells and eyes, leading to skin cancer and eye conditions.

core.h: Hazards of X-rays and gamma rays
core.p: X-rays and gamma rays are far more **penetrating** than ultraviolet. They pass through skin into the body, so they can damage cells in internal organs.
bullets: They are **ionising**, so they can cause **mutation of genes** (DNA) and **cancer**.
High doses **kill cells**, causing radiation burns and radiation sickness.
Rapidly dividing cells (bone marrow, gut lining, reproductive cells, a developing baby) are most at risk.
Damage to reproductive cells could cause mutations passed on to offspring.
Gamma rays usually have even higher frequencies than X-rays, so they can be even more damaging.

callouts.p: Say the mechanism: ionisation damages DNA, causing mutations that can lead to cancer. 'It causes cancer' alone often scores only 1 mark.

core.h: Comparing the three hazards
core.p: All three are harmful, but they differ in where they act and how penetrating they are.
bullets: UV is absorbed near the surface, so its effects are on skin and eyes.
X-rays and gamma rays pass deep into the body and affect internal organs.
Penetration and energy both increase from UV to X-rays to gamma rays.

core.h: What affects the size of the risk
core.p: The harm done is not fixed: it depends on how much radiation is absorbed and what type it is.
bullets: **Frequency (type) of radiation**: higher frequency means more energy and more damage.
**Intensity / dose**: more radiation absorbed means more chance of damage.
**Duration of exposure**: longer exposure gives a bigger dose.
**Part of the body** exposed: some organs are more sensitive.
Radiation dose is measured in **sieverts (Sv)**, usually millisieverts (mSv); it takes account of the type of radiation and the harm it causes.
Everyone receives a small background dose each year; medical doses are chosen so the benefit outweighs the small extra risk.

callouts.p: A good 3-mark answer names: type/frequency, dose (amount), and time of exposure.

core.h: Protecting people from ultraviolet
core.p: Because UV is absorbed at the surface, simple barriers block it.
bullets: **Sunscreen** absorbs or reflects UV before it reaches skin cells; a higher SPF gives more protection.
Covering skin with **clothing** and hats, and staying in the **shade** in the middle of the day.
**Sunglasses** that block UV protect the eyes from cataracts.
Limiting the use of **sunbeds**.
Welders wear protective visors because welding arcs emit intense UV.

core.h: Protecting people from X-rays and gamma rays
core.p: These rays are penetrating, so dense **shielding**, **distance** and short **time** of exposure are used.
bullets: **Lead** absorbs X-rays and gamma rays well: radiographers wear lead aprons and stand behind lead screens or leave the room.
Patients have parts of the body not being imaged covered with lead.
Exposure times are kept as short as possible and the number of scans limited.
Workers wear **dosimeter badges** to monitor the total dose they receive.
Gamma sources are stored in lead-lined containers and handled remotely or with tongs.
In radiotherapy, beams are aimed from several directions so healthy tissue receives a lower dose than the tumour.

callouts.p: Lead is very dense, so it absorbs X-rays and gamma rays strongly, reducing the dose that passes through.

core.h: Benefits versus risks
core.p: The same properties that make these waves hazardous make them useful. Decisions about using them balance benefit against risk.
bullets: A chest X-ray gives a tiny extra risk of cancer, much smaller than the benefit of diagnosing a disease.
Radiotherapy uses the ability of gamma rays to kill cells, aimed at cancer cells.
UV sterilises water because it kills microbes, the same way it damages skin cells.
Patients usually receive occasional doses, so the benefit is high and risk low; staff are exposed often, so they must protect themselves much more carefully.

callouts.p: In 'evaluate' questions, give at least one benefit and one risk, then a justified conclusion.

core.h: Non-ionising waves are not hazard free
core.p: Although the spec focuses on UV, X-rays and gamma, exam questions sometimes ask why the other regions are less dangerous.
bullets: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared and visible light have lower frequencies and **do not cause ionisation**.
Their main hazard is **heating** of tissue at high intensity, for example infrared burns or high-power microwaves.
Very bright visible light (such as lasers) can damage the retina.
They do not cause gene mutations in the way ionising radiation does.

callouts.p: Mobile phones and microwave ovens use non-ionising radiation, so they do not cause mutations by ionisation.

analogy.t: Thrown balls and a glass window
analogy.p: Imagine throwing balls at a window. Low-frequency radiation is like a stream of soft sponge balls: lots can hit without breaking anything, though they may warm it slightly. Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are like stones: each one has enough energy to crack the glass (ionise an atom and damage DNA). UV stones are small and only chip the surface (skin and eyes); X-rays and gamma are heavy stones that smash deep inside. The analogy breaks down because radiation energy is carried in packets whose energy depends on frequency, not on speed, and damaged cells can sometimes repair themselves.

terms.d: Electromagnetic radiation with a frequency just higher than visible light; absorbed by skin and eyes.
High-frequency, short-wavelength ionising electromagnetic radiation that passes through soft tissue.
The highest-frequency, most penetrating ionising electromagnetic radiation, emitted from unstable nuclei.
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz); higher frequency means more energy transferred.
The removal (or addition) of electrons from an atom or molecule, producing an ion.
Radiation with enough energy to ionise atoms; includes UV, X-rays and gamma rays.
An atom or molecule with an electrical charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
A change in the DNA (genes) of a cell, which can be caused by ionising radiation.
A disease in which mutated cells divide uncontrollably, forming tumours.
Clouding of the lens of the eye, which can be caused by exposure to ultraviolet.
How far radiation can travel into a material before being absorbed.
A measure of the harm caused by the radiation absorbed by the body, measured in sieverts (Sv).
The unit of radiation dose; 1 mSv = 0.001 Sv.
A dense material such as lead or concrete placed between a source and people to absorb radiation.
A badge worn by workers to measure the total radiation dose they receive.

mistakes.w: UV causes cancer of internal organs.
mistakes.r: UV is absorbed by surface cells, so it causes skin cancer and eye damage; X-rays and gamma rays affect internal organs.

mistakes.w: X-rays are dangerous because they make you radioactive.
mistakes.r: X-rays are ionising and can damage DNA, causing mutations and cancer; the patient does not become radioactive.

mistakes.w: High wavelength radiation is more dangerous.
mistakes.r: Shorter wavelength, higher frequency radiation transfers more energy and is more dangerous.

mistakes.w: Radiation causes cancer (with no mechanism).
mistakes.r: Ionising radiation ionises atoms in DNA, causing mutations that can lead to uncontrolled cell division (cancer).

mistakes.w: Sunscreen stops all harmful radiation including X-rays.
mistakes.r: Sunscreen absorbs or reflects UV only; X-rays and gamma need dense shielding such as lead.

mistakes.w: Microwaves and radio waves cause gene mutations.
mistakes.r: They are non-ionising; their hazard is heating at high intensity.

mistakes.w: Radiographers stay in the room to calm the patient.
mistakes.r: Radiographers leave the room or stand behind lead screens to reduce their exposure because they take many X-rays each day.

mistakes.w: Ionisation means atoms gain energy and get hot.
mistakes.r: Ionisation means electrons are removed from atoms, forming charged ions.

exam.q: Name one type of electromagnetic radiation that can cause skin cancer.
model: Ultraviolet (UV).
exam.tip: Also accept X-rays or gamma if the question says 'cancer' generally; skin cancer points to UV.

exam.q: State one effect of ultraviolet radiation on the eyes.
model: Damage to the eye / cataracts / snow blindness.
exam.tip: Be specific: 'eye conditions' or 'cataracts'.

exam.q: Explain why gamma rays are more hazardous than visible light.
model: Gamma rays have a higher frequency so transfer more energy.
Gamma rays are ionising (visible light is not), so they can damage cells / DNA.
exam.tip: Compare frequency then link to ionisation.

exam.q: Explain how X-rays can cause cancer.
model: X-rays are ionising radiation.
They can ionise atoms in DNA / damage genes in cells.
This causes mutations, which may make cells divide uncontrollably (cancer).
exam.tip: Follow the chain: ionise, damage DNA, mutation, cancer.

exam.q: Suggest two ways people can reduce their risk of harm from ultraviolet radiation.
model: Use sunscreen / sun cream with high SPF.
Wear clothing, a hat or UV-blocking sunglasses / stay in the shade / avoid sunbeds.
exam.tip: Two different methods for two marks.

exam.q: A radiographer takes many X-ray images each day. Explain why she stands behind a lead screen but the patient does not need to.
model: The radiographer would be exposed many times a day, so her total dose would be large.
Lead absorbs X-rays, reducing her dose.
The patient is exposed only occasionally; the benefit of the image outweighs the small risk.
exam.tip: Contrast frequency of exposure.

exam.q: State three factors that affect the amount of harm done by ionising radiation.
model: The type / frequency of radiation.
The dose / intensity absorbed.
The time of exposure (or the part of the body exposed).
exam.tip: Dose, time and type is a memorable trio.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by ionisation.
model: Removal of electrons from atoms (or molecules) to form ions.
exam.tip: Must mention electrons.

exam.q: Discuss the hazards of ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays to the human body, and how people can be protected from each.
model: All three are high frequency so transfer large amounts of energy / are ionising.
UV is absorbed by surface cells: causes sunburn, skin ageing, skin cancer, eye conditions such as cataracts.
Protection from UV: sunscreen, clothing, sunglasses, shade.
X-rays and gamma are penetrating, reach internal organs, ionise DNA causing mutations and cancer; high doses kill cells.
Protection: lead shielding, distance, limiting exposure time, dosimeter badges.
Harm depends on dose and duration of exposure.
exam.tip: Level 3: hazards AND protection for all three, with the ionisation mechanism explained.

exam.q: Explain why ultraviolet affects mainly the skin and eyes but gamma rays can damage internal organs.
model: Ultraviolet is absorbed by the outer layers of skin / is not very penetrating.
Gamma rays are highly penetrating so pass through the skin into the body.
exam.tip: The key word is penetration.

worked.q: A CT scan gives a dose of about 10 mSv. The average UK background dose is about 2.7 mSv per year. How many years of background radiation is one CT scan equivalent to, and should a patient refuse it?
steps: Years equivalent = 10 / 2.7.
= 3.7 years (to 2 significant figures).
The extra risk of cancer from one scan is small.
The scan can detect serious illness, so the benefit usually outweighs the risk.
worked.ans: About 3.7 years of background radiation; the patient should normally accept it because the diagnostic benefit outweighs the small extra risk.

worked.q: Evaluate the use of a sunbed for tanning.
steps: Benefit: gives a tan quickly, which some people like; UV helps the skin make vitamin D.
Risk: UV damages surface skin cells, causing premature ageing and sunburn.
Risk: UV can cause mutations in skin cell DNA, increasing the risk of skin cancer; eyes can be damaged without goggles.
Conclusion: the cosmetic benefit is small compared with the increased cancer risk, so sunbed use should be limited or avoided.
worked.ans: The risks (skin cancer, eye damage, skin ageing) outweigh the cosmetic benefit, so sunbeds should be avoided or strictly limited, with eye protection.
